**MONTREAL, Canada (CNN)** — In one of the most bizarre and dramatic pit-lane incidents in modern Formula One history, reigning world champion Kimi Raikkonen was left bewildered and out of the race after McLaren’s Lewis Hamilton crashed directly into the back of his Ferrari during Sunday’s Canadian Grand Prix.

The drama unfolded on lap 19 at the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve following a Safety Car deployment. The field flooded into the pit lane for routine stops, setting up a frantic exit. 

Raikkonen and BMW Sauber’s Robert Kubica emerged from their pit stalls side-by-side, but were forced to bring their cars to a complete stop at the end of the pit lane, waiting for the red exit light to turn green. 

Hamilton, who was leading the race prior to the pit stops, accelerated down the pit lane, seemingly unaware of the stopped cars ahead. By the time the British driver realized the situation, it was too late. Hamilton locked up his brakes, sliding his McLaren directly into the rear of Raikkonen’s stationary Ferrari, destroying both cars' rear wings and ending both drivers' races on the spot.

To add to the chaos, Williams driver Nico Rosberg then lightly tapped the back of Hamilton’s McLaren seconds later.

A visibly frustrated Raikkonen stepped out of his damaged Ferrari, walked over to Hamilton's car, and pointed directly at the red light before walking back to the paddock.

"I don't know what to say. My car was fine, we had a great strategy, and then... well, everyone saw what happened," a disappointed Raikkonen told reporters after returning to the Ferrari garage. 

"It's hard to understand how you can hit a car that is stopped at a red light side-by-side with another car. It’s an unbelievable mistake. There was a red light, I stopped, and then I just felt a big hit from behind. It ruined my race, and it cost us a lot of points."

Hamilton, who had taken the championship lead coming into the weekend, was quick to accept responsibility for the collision and offered a swift apology to the Finn.

"I saw the red light, but by the time I reacted and hit the brakes, it was far too late," Hamilton admitted. "I locked up and slid into the back of Kimi. It was purely an accident, and I apologize to Kimi if I ruined his race. You never want to eliminate yourself and another driver like that."

The incident provoked a furious reaction from Ferrari Team Principal Stefano Domenicali, who lamented the loss of a near-certain victory or double-podium finish for the Scuderia.

"It is immensely frustrating and difficult to accept," Domenicali said. "It was an unbelievable mistake by Lewis. To see a race end like that for Kimi—when he was in a perfect position to win the race—is very hard to swallow. We were managing the race well, and to be taken out in the pit lane while waiting for a red light is something you just do not expect at this level."

Race stewards acted swiftly following the checkered flag, handing both Hamilton and Rosberg a 10-place grid penalty for the upcoming French Grand Prix at Magny-Cours.

The pit-lane disaster completely reshuffled the race, paving the way for BMW Sauber’s Robert Kubica to claim his maiden Formula One victory, leading a historic 1-2 finish for his team alongside teammate Nick Heidfeld. 

The result leaves the 2008 World Championship battle blown wide open, with Kubica now unexpectedly topping the driver standings, while Hamilton and Raikkonen are left to reflect on a disastrous afternoon in Montreal.

Formula 1 is a sport where split-second decisions are made at speeds exceeding 200 mph. Drivers possess superhuman reflexes, honed to react to the micro-adjustments of a car on the absolute edge of control. Yet, on Lap 19 of the 2008 Canadian Grand Prix, the world’s most sophisticated motorsport produced a moment straight out of a suburban traffic nightmare: a simple rear-end collision at a red light.

The victim was defending World Champion Kimi Räikkönen. The culprit was F1’s fast-rising sensation, Lewis Hamilton. The location was the exit of the Montreal pit lane. The result was one of the most bizarre and infamous blunders in modern Grand Prix history.

### The Setup: High Stakes in Montreal

Entering the 2008 Canadian Grand Prix at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve, the championship battle was fiercely contested. Hamilton, driving for McLaren, held a slender lead in the standings, while Ferrari’s Räikkönen was nipping at his heels. 

Hamilton had taken a brilliant pole position and dominated the opening stint of the race. But on Lap 15, Force India’s Adrian Sutil suffered a gearbox failure, bringing out the Safety Car. Under the rules of the era, the pit lane remained closed until the Safety Car pack bunched up, triggering a mad rush into the pits as soon as the pit lane opened on Lap 19.

Hamilton pitted from the lead, followed closely by BMW Sauber’s Robert Kubica and Ferrari’s Räikkönen. 

### The Pit Lane Pitfall

What followed was a masterclass in pit-crew efficiency—and ultimate driver distraction. 

Ferrari and BMW executed lightning-fast pit stops. Räikkönen and Kubica released side-by-side, edging ahead of Hamilton, whose McLaren stop was just a fraction of a second slower. The two cars surged down the long pit exit lane toward the track junction.

However, the pit lane regulations dictated that drivers had to wait for a green light at the exit, allowing the Safety Car queue on the main straight to pass safely before joining the circuit.

Recognizing the bright red light beaming over the track, Kubica and Räikkönen slammed on the brakes, stopping side-by-side at the line. 

Hamilton, rushing down the pit lane to regain his lost position, was looking elsewhere—checking his steering wheel display, searching for an opening, or simply caught off-guard by the stopped cars. By the time the young Briton realized what was happening, it was too late. 

Hamilton locked up his brakes, but his McLaren slid helplessly across the tarmac, plowing straight into the back of Räikkönen’s Ferrari, crushing the Finn's rear wing. To add comedy to tragedy, Williams driver Nico Rosberg, also caught unawares, slid into the back of Hamilton’s McLaren seconds later.

### "He Hit Me From Behind at a Red Light"

The visual was surreal. Three of the fastest cars in the world were crumpled together in a heap at a standstill, safely tucked away in the pit exit, while the rest of the field zoomed past.

Hamilton and Räikkönen immediately climbed out of their ruined machines. Räikkönen, famous for his stoic "Iceman" demeanor, walked over to the rear of his car, calmly pointed at the blaring red light, and offered Hamilton a gesture of utter bewilderment. 

In the post-race interviews, Räikkönen didn’t hide his frustration, though he delivered his verdict with his typical matter-of-fact dry humor:
*"My race was ruined by Hamilton,"* Räikkönen said. *"Obviously, everybody can make mistakes, like I did two weeks ago in Monaco, but it is one thing to make a mistake on the track and another to hit someone stopped at a red light."*

Hamilton was deeply apologetic, admitting the fault lay entirely on his shoulders. 
*"I saw the red light, but by the time I hit the brakes, it was too late,"* Hamilton explained. *"It was just one of those things. I saw them stopping, but it was too late to avoid them. It’s a shame, but I apologize to Kimi if I ruined his race."*

### The Aftermath and Historical Twist

The race stewards took a dim view of the incident. Both Hamilton and Rosberg were handed 10-place grid penalties for the following race in France. 

While the incident was a disaster for Hamilton and Ferrari, it paved the way for a fairytale story. Robert Kubica, who had wisely stopped next to Räikkönen and avoided the carnage, went on to win the race. It was Kubica’s first and only Formula 1 victory—coming exactly one year after he had survived a terrifying, violent crash at the very same circuit. 

Hamilton would ultimately have the last laugh that season, overcoming the Montreal embarrassment to win his agonizingly dramatic first World Championship in Brazil later that year.

Yet, despite all of Hamilton’s eventual 100+ race wins and seven World Titles, the 2008 Canadian GP remains an indelible footprint in his career narrative—a reminder that even the greatest drivers in history aren't immune to the most basic driving errors.

**DRAMA IN MONTREAL: Hamilton Pit-Lane Calamity Hands Victory to Kubica as FIA Hands Down Heavy Penalty**

**By CNN Sport F1 Desk**
**MONTREAL, Canada —** In one of the most astonishing pit-lane blunders in modern Formula One history, a moment of madness at the 2008 Canadian Grand Prix saw championship leader Lewis Hamilton crash directly into the back of reigning world champion Kimi Räikkönen, knocking both out of the race and altering the course of the world championship.

What was shaping up to be a tactical masterclass at the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve descended into pure chaos on Lap 19 following a Safety Car deployment to clear Adrian Sutil’s stalled Force India. 

As the leaders dived into the pit lane, Hamilton, who had been leading comfortably from pole position, suffered a slightly slower pit stop than his rivals. Ferrari’s Räikkönen and BMW Sauber’s Robert Kubica managed to leapfrog the McLaren driver in the pit lane. 

The two drivers accelerated toward the pit exit, only to find a red light glowing brightly—a signal indicating that the pit exit was closed while the Safety Car train passed on the main straight. Both Räikkönen and Kubica came to a controlled, side-by-side stop at the line.

Hamilton, however, failed to notice the illuminated red signal in time. 

Approaching at speed, the 23-year-old Briton locked up his brakes far too late, slamming his McLaren squarely into the back of Räikkönen’s stationary Ferrari. Moments later, Williams’ Nico Rosberg piled into the back of Hamilton, completing a bizarre, multi-car pileup in the pit lane.

Both Hamilton and Räikkönen suffered catastrophic suspension and rear-end damage, forcing their immediate retirement from the race. Kubica, standing just inches away in the adjacent pit lane line, miraculously escaped unscathed.

### **The Reactions: Disbelief, Frustration, and Remorse**

The aftermath of the crash provided one of the most iconic visual moments of the season. A visibly furious Räikkönen stepped out of his damaged Ferrari, walked over to Hamilton’s cockpit, and pointed emphatically toward the glaring red pit exit light, ensuring the young Englishman knew precisely what he had done.

Speaking to reporters after returning to the paddock, Räikkönen did little to hide his frustration, lamenting a lost opportunity for Ferrari.

"My race was ruined by Hamilton's mistake," a sullen Räikkönen said. "When the light is red, you stop. It’s as simple as that. I saw the light, I stopped, and then I just felt a big hit on the back of my car. I couldn't believe it. It’s hard to understand how someone can make a mistake like that in the pit lane."

Hamilton was apologetic, admitting total fault for the collision while explaining how the rapid sequence of events caught him off guard.

"It’s just one of those things," Hamilton told CNN. "I was trying to look at the guys leaving the pits, trying to get out ahead of them, and by the time I saw the red light, it was too late. I locked up and couldn't avoid Kimi. I apologize to him; it’s never my intention to ruin anyone’s race, let alone my own. It’s a lesson learned."

Kubica, who watched the drama unfold in his side-view mirror, offered a understated perspective on his near-miss. 

"I saw the red light and stopped, and Kimi stopped next to me," Kubica said. "Suddenly I heard a loud crash. I looked in the mirror and saw Lewis in the back of Kimi. I just thought, 'I need to get out of here when the light turns green.' It was crazy."

### **The FIA Penalty**

Following a post-race investigation by the FIA Race Stewards, the governing body delivered a swift and stern punishment for the breach of Article 31.1 of the F1 Sporting Regulations.

Both **Lewis Hamilton** and **Nico Rosberg** were handed **10-place grid penalties** for the upcoming French Grand Prix at Magny-Cours. The stewards deemed Hamilton entirely at fault for causing an avoidable collision in a designated low-speed zone.

The penalty serves as a massive blow to Hamilton’s championship aspirations, forcing him to fight from the middle of the pack in France.

### **A Historic Silver Lining**

While McLaren and Ferrari were left to pick up the pieces of a ruined afternoon, the pit-lane melee opened the door for a fairy-tale ending for BMW Sauber. 

Robert Kubica navigated the remainder of the race flawlessly to secure his **first-ever Formula One victory**—and the first in the history of the BMW Sauber team. To cap off an extraordinary day, Kubica’s teammate Nick Heidfeld finished second, securing a historic 1-2 finish for the German-Swiss outfit.

With the victory, Kubica unexpectedly vaulted to the top of the Drivers’ World Championship standings, adding yet another layer of intrigue to an already volatile 2008 season. 

As the paddock packs up to return to Europe, the headlines from Montreal will undoubtedly belong to Lewis Hamilton’s lapse in judgment—a costly red-light blunder that will reverberate through the championship fight for weeks to come.

**MONTREAL PIT DRAMA: Hamilton Apologizes After Bizarre Pit Lane Crash Ruins Räikkönen’s Canadian GP**

**MONTREAL, Canada** — McLaren’s Lewis Hamilton offered a full apology to Kimi Räikkönen after a bizarre and costly pit lane collision forced both championship contenders out of the Canadian Grand Prix, leaving the Ferrari driver lamenting a lost opportunity for victory. 

The extraordinary incident occurred on lap 19 under Safety Car conditions. Following a round of pit stops, reigning World Champion Räikkönen and BMW Sauber’s Robert Kubica brought their cars to a halt side-by-side at the end of the pit lane, waiting for the red exit light to turn green. 

Hamilton, who had entered the pits as the race leader, failed to notice the stopped cars and the red signal in time. The British driver locked up his brakes and plowed directly into the rear of Räikkönen’s Ferrari, destroying both cars' rear and front wings respectively. To add to the chaos, Williams driver Nico Rosberg then bumped into the back of Hamilton.

Räikkönen, whose car suffered irreparable rear-end damage, famously climbed out of his Ferrari and pointed toward the illuminated red light to highlight the mistake to a remorseful Hamilton. 

Speaking to reporters after returning to the paddock, a visibly frustrated Räikkönen did not hide his disappointment at being knocked out of a race he felt he was in a strong position to win.

"My car was very good today, and we were in a great position to get a result," said the Iceman, maintaining his trademark calm demeanor despite the clear irritation. "When the light turns red, you stop. It’s as simple as that. I was sitting there alongside Kubica waiting for the green, and suddenly I was hit from behind. There was nothing I could do. It’s hard to understand how someone can hit you when you are standing still at a red light."

Hamilton was quick to take responsibility for the blunder, admitting he simply spotted the red light too late while attempting to negotiate the exit speed.

"It was just one of those things," Hamilton explained. "I saw the red light, but by the time I hit the brakes, it was too late. I’m sorry for Kimi if I ruined his race. It’s not how you want a race to end, and it’s obviously very frustrating for the team, but I accept full responsibility. It was a mistake."

Race stewards acted swiftly following the grand prix, handing both Hamilton and Rosberg ten-place grid penalties for the upcoming French Grand Prix at Magny-Cours. 

The double retirement reshuffled the 2008 World Championship narrative significantly. Kubica, who narrowly avoided the melee beside Räikkönen, went on to secure a sensational maiden Formula 1 victory for BMW Sauber, taking the lead in the Drivers' Championship in the process.

For Räikkönen, the pit lane disaster marks a zero-point weekend that severely damages his title defense momentum, while Hamilton leaves Montreal searching for answers after a weekend that promised victory ended in embarrassment.
